section.title: Problem
section.p: Froth has moved in the right direction. RFC-0008 correctly unified telemetry_events and agent_events into one events table. But the current ontology still carries the scars of the older split world.
The database still treats too many things as separate species of truth:

item.p: events for telemetry and agent runtime facts
tasks plus task_events for background work
agent_cycles and agent_messages for cycles and transcript state
telegram_cycle_links and task_telegram_links for app-specific relations
codex_session_events as another event universe beside events

section.p: This does not merely create extra tables. It creates extra ontologies. The system has to keep re-explaining to itself whether something is an event, a task, a cycle, a message, a session, a transcript row, a link row, or a projection. That is exactly the sort of conceptual tax that later appears as confused prompts, heuristic joins, duplicate readers, and ugly adapter code.

The naming also reveals the problem. The events table is already carrying more than happenings. Some rows are durable records or ledgers. The metadata column is often not metadata at all. It is the actual payload.

section.title: Goal
section.p: Reduce Froth's core runtime ontology to two truths and one discipline:

item.p: facts — append-only records of things that are true
links — append-only named relations between facts
projections are disposable — any optimized read model is derived, rebuildable, and not the source of truth

section.p: The result should be simpler than the current world, not more abstract in a way that only moves the confusion elsewhere.

section.title: Thesis
section.p: The next simplification after RFC-0008 is not another unification pass around the word "event". It is a more general ontology.

Froth should stop distinguishing so sharply between "event" rows and "object" rows. A message, a tool invocation, a tool result, a task snapshot, a notification, a user profile, an analysis artifact, and a cycle completion are all facts. Some facts describe happenings. Some facts describe entities. Some facts describe derived state. That distinction belongs in kind and payload, not in the table model itself.

Relations should be explicit and first-class rather than smuggled into special columns and app-specific link tables. Span trees, parent chains, task-to-cycle attachment, reply edges, derivation edges, and provenance edges are all the same species of thing: links.

subsection.title: 1. Facts replace the narrow event/object split
subsection.p: Introduce a core table called facts. This may begin as a rename or successor to the current events table.
subsection.code: facts id uuid/text NOT NULL primary key kind text NOT NULL payload jsonb NOT NULL default '{}' inserted_at timestamp NOT NULL
subsection.p: There may later be convenience columns that are truly universal. But the burden of proof should be high. The point is to stop baking domain-specific assumptions into the base schema.

item.p: rename event to kind
rename metadata to payload
treat "objectness" as just another kind of fact, not a separate storage class

subsection.title: 2. Links replace special-case relation columns and tables
subsection.p: Introduce a core table called links:
subsection.code: links id uuid/text NOT NULL primary key from_id uuid/text NOT NULL predicate text NOT NULL to_id uuid/text NOT NULL payload jsonb NOT NULL default '{}' inserted_at timestamp NOT NULL
subsection.p: The relation names should be ontological rather than schema-shaped. Prefer predicates like:

item.p: parent_of or child_of where true parentage matters

subsection.p: Avoid schema-shaped predicates like belongs_to_cycle when a more general predicate such as part_of expresses the truth better.
Under this model, current columns and tables like span_id, parent_id, telegram_cycle_links, and task_telegram_links become links instead of bespoke subsystems.

subsection.title: 3. Projections are allowed, but demoted
subsection.p: This RFC is not a purity cult. Froth will still want optimized read models.
Examples of projections that may remain useful:

item.p: current task state
cycle summaries
timeline views for UI
search indexes
lease tables or uniqueness guards

subsection.p: But those projections should be understood as caches, views, or materialized summaries over facts and links. They are not separate truths with their own ontology.

subsection.title: 4. The current `events` table is the right ancestor
subsection.p: The existing events table is already closer to the correct core than most of the rest of the schema. It is append-only, flexible, and heavily used. The direction here is not to repudiate RFC-0008. It is to generalize it.
The most obvious immediate improvements are:

item.p: rename the semantic surface from events/event/metadata to facts/kind/payload
move relation columns such as span_id and parent_id out of the base fact table and into links
stop creating fresh event-like universes such as codex_session_events when they can instead be fact kinds with links

subsection.title: 5. Example
subsection.p: A delegated sub-agent run might look like:
subsection.code:
fact kind=agent.cycle fact kind=tool.invocation fact kind=tool.result fact kind=telegram.message fact kind=task.state
link predicate=part_of tool.invocation -> agent.cycle link predicate=caused_by tool.result -> tool.invocation link predicate=part_of task.state -> agent.cycle link predicate=reply_to telegram.message -> telegram.message link predicate=derived_from telegram.message -> tool.result
subsection.p: No extra ontology is needed to explain why one of those is a task, another is a cycle, and another is a message. They are all facts. Their meaning comes from kind and their links.

section.title: Migration Strategy
section.p: This should land as a gradual architectural migration, not a theology-driven table purge.

item.p: Rename the mental model first in docs and readers: prefer kind and payload vocabulary over event and metadata.
Introduce links and start writing explicit relations for new subsystems instead of adding bespoke link tables and relation columns.
Mirror high-value existing edges such as span parentage, cycle attachment, reply edges, and task attachment into links.
Collapse parallel event stores where practical, especially ones that are semantically just fact streams under a different name.
Move optimized readers onto projections derived from facts and links.
Only after the projections are stable should old special-case tables be retired.

section.p: The important ordering rule is: change ontology before changing storage aggressively. Froth should first stop thinking in the old categories, then simplify the schema beneath that new understanding.

section.title: Performance
section.p: This design is intentionally willing to postpone specialization.
If the ontology is right, performance problems can be met with:

item.p: indexes
materialized views
projection tables
partial indexes by kind or predicate
cached hot-path summaries

section.p: If the ontology is wrong, no amount of indexing makes the system pleasant to reason about.
The rule should therefore be: tolerate some inefficiency in the core truth model, and optimize only after real suffering appears.

item.p: Froth gets one simpler ontology instead of many overlapping ones.
Agent-facing tools can converge on one primary handle and one inspection model.
App-specific link tables and relation columns become replaceable with a generic graph.
New subsystems no longer need to invent their own event stores just to persist a timeline.
Terms like "task", "cycle", and "session" become kinds and projections, not rival universes.
Queries become more abstract until projections are in place.
Some invariants that were once implicit in table shape must be enforced in code or projection logic.
There will be a migration period where the old schema and the new ontology coexist uneasily.

section.title: Recommendation
section.p: The long-term core of Froth should be facts and links, with projections treated as secondary and disposable.

Do not chase this by immediately deleting half the database. Do chase it by refusing to add new ontologies lightly, by renaming the existing core in a more truthful way, and by making relations explicit and generic rather than bespoke.
